title: Ancient Sea-Going Armored Amphibian Discovered: 237‑Million‑Year‑Old Fossils Reveal Marine Lifestyle
body:
A team of paleontologists has uncovered the remains of a previously unknown amphibian that spent its entire life in the open ocean, pushing back the timeline for fully marine tetrapods to the Middle Triassic, about 237 million years ago. The creature, described as a heavily armored, salamander‑sized bottom dweller, represents the earliest known example of an amphibian that abandoned freshwater habitats altogether and adapted to life beneath the waves.

The fossils, recovered from marine deposits in southwestern China’s Guizhou Province, include a near‑complete skeleton with a distinctive shield of bony plates covering its back and tail. Detailed analysis of the bone microstructure and the surrounding sediment indicates the animal lived in a shallow, low‑oxygen seafloor environment, feeding on benthic invertebrates. Its robust limbs and flattened body suggest a lifestyle similar to modern lungfish or certain salamanders that cling to the substrate, but the presence of a fully developed lateral line system and reinforced vertebrae point to a long‑term marine existence rather than a temporary foray into salty water.

“This discovery rewrites our understanding of early amphibian ecology,” said Dr. Jianhua Liu, a senior researcher at the University of California, Davis, who led the study. “Until now, the consensus was that amphibians remained tied to freshwater or brackish habitats after their initial transition from fish. The armor and anatomical features of this specimen show a lineage that not only tolerated saltwater but fully embraced it, evolving specialized defenses against predators and the harsh conditions of the ancient seas.” The researchers propose the animal belongs to a previously unrecognized group within the order Temnospondyli, a diverse clade that dominated amphibian life in the Paleozoic and early Mesozoic eras.

The find also sheds light on the broader evolutionary experimentations occurring after the Permian‑Triassic extinction, the most severe biodiversity loss in Earth’s history. In the wake of that crisis, many lineages explored new ecological niches, and the emergence of a marine amphibian underscores the adaptive flexibility of early tetrapods. While reptiles would later dominate marine environments, this amphibian demonstrates that the evolutionary race to colonize the oceans was not limited to the ancestors of modern whales, turtles, and sea snakes.

Comparisons with contemporaneous marine reptiles, such as the early ichthyosaurs, reveal striking convergences. Both groups developed streamlined bodies and protective armor, albeit through different developmental pathways. However, the amphibian’s reliance on cutaneous respiration—a hallmark of modern amphibians—suggests it may have been constrained to oxygen‑poor waters where its skin could efficiently absorb dissolved gases. This physiological limitation likely kept it near the seafloor, contrasting with the pelagic habits of later marine reptiles.

The discovery opens new avenues for research into the genetic and developmental mechanisms that enabled amphibians to tolerate saline environments. Future excavations in Triassic marine strata across the globe could uncover related species, helping scientists map the spread and diversification of marine amphibians before they vanished from the fossil record. As paleontologists continue to piece together the puzzle of life’s early ventures onto the seas, this armored bottom‑dweller stands as a vivid reminder that the evolutionary story of marine vertebrates is far more intricate than previously imagined.
